content: Hyaluronan synthase 1 (HAS1) is an enzyme encoded by the HAS1 gene in humans. Hyaluronan, also known as hyaluronic acid (HA), is a high molecular weight, unbranched polysaccharide that is synthesized by a wide range of organisms, including bacteria and mammals. It is a key component of the extracellular matrix. The structure of HA consists of repeating disaccharide units made up of glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine. These units are connected by beta-1,3 and beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds. The synthesis of HA occurs at the inner surface of the plasma membrane, where it is produced by a membrane-bound synthase enzyme. Once synthesized, the HA chains are transported into the extracellular space via an ABC transporter. HA performs several critical biological functions. It acts as a space-filling molecule, provides lubrication in joints, and forms a structural matrix that facilitates cell migration. During processes such as wound healing and tissue repair, HA is actively synthesized to create a scaffold that supports the ingrowth of blood vessels and fibroblasts. Alterations in serum HA levels are associated with inflammatory and degenerative joint diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis. Furthermore, HA interacts with the leukocyte receptor CD44, which plays a crucial role in tissue-specific leukocyte homing. Overexpression of HA receptors has been linked to tumor metastasis. HAS1 belongs to a recently identified family of vertebrate genes that encode hyaluronan synthases. The amino acid sequence of HAS1 shares significant homology with the hasA gene product of Streptococcus pyogenes, a glycosaminoglycan synthetase (DG42) from Xenopus laevis, and a murine hyaluronan synthase that has been described in recent studies.
